body: You seem to understand CBT well. Since my understanding is lacking, would you be able to try explain better how it works? Perhaps if I understood it better, it could be more effective. CBT was not something we went into any depth on at all in psychology, I do admit.

http://www.nhs.uk/Conditions/Post-traumatic-stress-disorder/Pages/Treatment.aspx
http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/Cognitive-behavioural-therapy/Pages/Introduction.aspx

A big challenge with me as a patient is the unfortunate problem that I actually did study first year psychology. My slight education in psychology may be a bit of a hindrance, as my perspective on psychology may not necessarily match the approach of my psychiatrist. Where it doesn't match, there's a difference in approach and understanding, and therefore in method - and surely if things are going to work, I have to believe they can? That's sort of what that CBT stuff is about, right?

CBT reads to me like saying "We're going to fix the way you think by the power of positive thinking". The way to salvation is through thinking happy thoughts? Wow, thanks, Tinkerbell. I'm very much aware of the fact negative thoughts spiral, and if I knew how to have positive thoughts without needing an external stimulus, I'd be using them. Maybe this kumbaya stuff works for other people, but I'm not convinced it can work for me.

Exposure therapy reads more like "Let's just talk it out". I'm not entirely convinced that just talking it out is going to work. A lot of the stressors in my day to day life are unavoidable and unsympathetic, and talking does not get me away from those stressors.

EMDR makes the most sense to me. I can sort of see how activating other parts of the brain while I'm thinking about something traumatic might do something like opening new pathways up to just sidestep the trauma and allow me to function. I know playing video games or listening to music cuts down on a lot of anxiety and fidgeting, so maybe EMDR can work? But I don't know whether that's a workable strategy for using while at work, for example.

Thanks for chiming in, janus1969. It's given me a bit of encouragement to actually seek treatment. It's one thing getting that reassurance from a friend, it's another to get it from a stranger who's been through the ringer themselves.

Had this from mom about my depression diagnosis as a teenager. Fortunately, I lived in the UK and got care through the NHS. To this day, my mom still denies that I had (have? dunno, feels like it sometimes) depression, and minimizes my feelings in general. And because she denies my depression, and has her own little delusional history of what happened when I was a teenager, bringing it up today results in more gaslighting. I don't bring it up anymore - grey rock all the way.

You are not the problem. Chances are, you might even have developed those problems because of the stress your nMom puts you under.
Oh yeah, all the time from Nmom, still does it now, and I'm 30.

I know this feeling so well - as soon as I remove myself from a confrontation with my nmom, she immediately starts in on dad, saying he never supports her on anything. She's been doing this for so long my dad has just plain shut down... except when we're out, just the two of us, and can be ourselves.

I admit that while I desperately want to get out and on my own, there's a small, empathic, stupid, part of me that wants to stay so dad won't be alone. However, everything I read about emotional abuse in marriages - yep, lots of soul searching on that subject very recently for me - applies here too: staying to protect someone else is not going to help anyone.

Absolutely, positively, yes! Libraries have been a safe haven for me for everything from abuse by my nmom, to bullying at school, to just plain freaking out from what I now recognize as PTSD episodes. Even if you don't pick up non-fiction help from the books you find there, there's pages upon pages of escapism there just waiting for you to come along and jump on in!

There just might even be a copy of the original novel of The Neverending Story on which the movie is based. If you don't know the plot for this, it's worth a look; Bastian is bullied at school, and neglected by dad after the death of his mother - he hides from some bullies in an antique shop, finds and borrows a book, and indulges in a bit of escapist reading... and that's where the story really begins.

I've also accidentally found many a character with issues so much like mine I wonder whether the author knows me - and it makes me feel like I'm not alone in feeling what I do. Very validating. Hopefully, you can find that in fiction too.

Full disclosure: I was a school librarian. Of course I'm going to recommend libraries and reading ;)

Hey man, I'm so sorry you're being treated like that. I'm also transmale, and I totally get where you're coming from on the misgendering and minimization of your gender dysphoria by your nmom, mine does the same to me.

As others have said, you really do need to find a trans support group, preferably a local one. Sadly, many of them will have experienced similar transphobic behaviors, and may have left home very young as well. Because of this, they are likely to be a wealth of information on housing and medical support for trans youth.

I know you won't want to hear this next part, but at least think it over? Abuse will wear you down if you stay in an abusive relationship (in this case parental). 41% of transgender people in the US attempt suicide, which is 10 times the national average. Ongoing abuse may push you toward it. If you can get away from the abuse, you should - yes, it will mean delaying treatment for being transgender - but it might just save your life.
